l: GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, front matter .. GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation / Abstract
s: Yuntong Hu, Zhihan Lei, Zheng Zhang, Bo Pan, Chen Ling, and Liang Zhao introduce Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GRAG). GRAG addresses the limitations of Naive Retrieval-Augmented Generation in handling networked documents by retrieving textual subgraphs and integrating textual and topological information into Large Language Models. The authors propose a divide-and-conquer strategy for efficient linear-time subgraph retrieval and use text and graph views for graph context-aware generation. Experiments on graph reasoning benchmarks show that GRAG significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art RAG methods in multi-hop reasoning on textual graphs.

l: GRAG, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, front matter .. GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation / Abstract
s: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GRAG) is introduced to retrieve textual subgraphs and integrate their joint textual and topological information into Large Language Models. It uses a divide-and-conquer strategy for linear-time subgraph retrieval and incorporates textual graphs through text and graph views.

l: GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Introduction
s: This unit concerns how Large Language Models (LLMs) can use networked documents for retrieval and generation. It introduces Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GRAG), which extends Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) by incorporating graph context during both retrieval and generation. GRAG retrieves relevant textual subgraphs through ego-graph retrieval followed by graph soft pruning, and provides their information to LLMs through hierarchical text descriptions and graph-based soft prompts. Experiments on graph multi-hop reasoning benchmarks show that GRAG outperforms RAG-based retrievers and LLM baselines, with frozen LLMs using GRAG outperforming fine-tuned LLMs on all tasks.

l: large language model, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Introduction
s: Large Language Models demonstrate capabilities in various reasoning tasks, including graph-based data, but struggle with factual errors because of limitations in training data and lack of real-time knowledge. In this unit, they are provided with textual and graph prompts through GRAG to improve understanding of relationships in networked documents.

l: graph-based reasoning, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Introduction
s: Graph-based reasoning is identified as a task on which Large Language Models have demonstrated capabilities. The unit evaluates GRAG in graph reasoning scenarios and reports that it outperforms RAG-based retrievers and LLM baselines.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Introduction
s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation integrates external data retrieval into the generative process to provide LLMs with relevant information and reduce factual errors. Traditional approaches focus on retrieving individual documents based on text similarity and do not explicitly account for document networks.

l: GRAG, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Introduction
s: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation extends Retrieval-Augmented Generation by incorporating graph context during retrieval and generation. It retrieves relevant textual subgraphs using ego-graph retrieval and graph soft pruning, then supplies hierarchical text descriptions as hard prompts and graph-encoder outputs as soft prompts.

l: networked documents, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Introduction
s: Documents such as social media postings, research papers, knowledge items, and product reviews are described as networked rather than isolated. Their relationships can be important for retrieving comprehensive information and for generating answers that reflect the surrounding context.

l: textual graph, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Introduction
s: Textual graphs represent networked documents with textual features in nodes and edges. They are used by GRAG to preserve both textual and topological information during retrieval and generation.

l: textual subgraphs, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Introduction
s: A textual subgraph is the target of GRAG retrieval rather than a set of discrete entities or individual documents. Retrieving it is challenging because textual nodes and edges create a high-dimensional combinatorial optimization problem, so GRAG uses an approximate divide-and-conquer strategy.

l: graph context, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Introduction
s: Graph context is incorporated into both the retrieval and generation stages of GRAG. It is represented through hierarchical text descriptions and graph-based soft prompts so that LLMs can use relationships and topology alongside textual information.

l: graph multi-hop reasoning benchmarks, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Introduction
s: Graph multi-hop reasoning benchmarks are used to evaluate GRAG. The reported experiments show that GRAG significantly outperforms current RAG methods and LLM baselines, while a frozen LLM with GRAG outperforms a fine-tuned LLM on all tasks.

l: GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2 / 2.1 .. 2.3
s: This unit reviews prompt tuning, emphasizing soft prompts that adapt task-specific behavior while preserving model parameters and extensions to multi-modal contexts. It describes how LLMs support graph-related tasks by encoding textual node and edge attributes, creating knowledge graphs, performing graph reasoning, and answering graph questions in zero-shot settings. The unit notes that LLMs do not inherently understand complex graph structure because text lacks explicit topological information. It also surveys retrieval on graphs, including retrieval of nodes, triples, paths, communities, and information combining textual and topological signals.

l: prompt tuning, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2 / 2.1 .. 2.3
s: Prompt tuning modifies inputs to guide model responses rather than updating model parameters. Lester et al. propose learning soft prompts directly as embeddings for task-specific adaptation while preserving the model's original parameters, and later work adapts prompt embeddings to multi-modal contexts.

l: large language model, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2 / 2.1 .. 2.3
s: LLMs encode textual node and edge attributes, benefiting classification and knowledge graph creation, while their contextual reasoning capabilities support graph reasoning and zero-shot graph answering. However, training on text does not inherently equip them to understand or reason about complex graph-structured data because textual data lacks explicit topological information.

l: graph multi-hop reasoning, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2 / 2.1 .. 2.3
s: LLMs are applied to graph-related tasks including classification, knowledge graph creation, graph reasoning, and zero-shot graph answering. Their effectiveness is supported by text embedding and contextual reasoning capabilities, but complex graph structures remain challenging.

l: graph prompt tuning, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2 / 2.1 .. 2.3
s: Graph prompt tuning has recently emerged as a tool for helping LLMs process and comprehend topological information.

l: retrieval on graphs, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2 / 2.1 .. 2.3
s: Retrieval on graphs includes retrieving relevant nodes, triples, paths, and communities to support answering graph-based questions. Retrieval methods also incorporate both textual and topological information to better capture structural relationships in graph-structured data.

l: graph-based reasoning, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2 / 2.1 .. 2.3
s: LLM contextual reasoning capabilities benefit graph reasoning. Some graph retrieval problems can be simplified into reasoning chains that retrieve the path between a question and a target entity.

l: textual and topological information, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 2 / 2.1 .. 2.3
s: Retrieval processes can incorporate both textual and topological information, allowing models to better capture structural relationships within graph-structured data.

l: GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3
s: The unit formalizes Textual Graphs as graphs with text-attributed nodes and edges. It defines Textual Subgraphs as subgraph structures formed from subsets of a textual graph's nodes and edges. Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation integrates graph context into retrieval and generation to improve the relevance of generated content. Given a query over a textual graph G, GRAG aims to retrieve an optimal textual subgraph ˆg and provide it with the query to LLMθ for answer generation.

l: textual graph, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3
s: Textual Graphs are formally defined as graphs consisting of text-attributed nodes and edges. They are represented by G = (V, E, {Tn}n∈V, {Te}e∈E), where V and E are the node and edge sets and Tn and Te are their natural language attributes.

l: textual subgraphs, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3
s: Textual Subgraphs are subgraph structures within a textual graph. They are formed using subsets of the graph's nodes and edges, together with the corresponding natural language attributes.

l: GRAG, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3
s: Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation integrates graph context into both retrieval and generation. Given a query over a textual graph, it aims to retrieve an optimal textual subgraph and incorporate its information into an LLM to improve the relevance of generated content.

l: textual graph G, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3
s: The textual graph G contains node and edge sets along with their natural language attributes. For a specific query q, its set of subgraphs S(G) is searched for a subgraph that supports answer generation aligned with expectations.

l: optimal textual subgraph ˆg, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3
s: The optimal textual subgraph ˆg is an element of S(G) that leads the LLM to generate answers aligned with expectations. GRAG retrieves ˆg and combines its information with the query during generation.

l: LLMθ, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 3
s: LLMθ is parameterized by θ and receives the query together with the optimal textual subgraph information. It generates the final output sequence token by token according to pθ(yi | y<i, [q, ˆg]).

l: GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: This unit introduces GRAG, a method for textual subgraph retrieval and generation. GRAG uses a divide-and-conquer strategy to retrieve important ego-graphs, merge the top-N relevant ones, and apply soft pruning to reduce redundant nodes and edges. It represents textual graphs through complementary graph and text views to preserve both topology and textual information. For retrieval, it indexes K-hop ego-graphs with embeddings from a pre-trained language model, ranks them by cosine similarity to the query, and selects promising candidate subgraphs for further refinement.

l: GRAG, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: GRAG addresses textual subgraph retrieval with a divide-and-conquer strategy. It retrieves important ego-graphs, merges the top-N relevant ones, and applies soft pruning to produce an approximately optimal subgraph while preserving textual and topological information.

l: textual subgraph retrieval, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: Textual subgraph retrieval seeks a subgraph that maximizes generation quality. The method approximates this NP-hard problem by selecting important nodes, retrieving their neighborhoods, ranking candidate ego-graphs, and refining the selected neighborhoods.

l: textual graph G, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: A textual graph contains textual attributes on nodes and edges. GRAG represents it through a graph view that preserves connections as soft prompts and a text view that converts it into hierarchical text descriptions as hard prompts.

l: optimal textual subgraph ˆg, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: The important subgraph is assumed to consist of important nodes and some of their neighbors. GRAG approximates it by merging partial neighborhoods around selected key nodes and pruning irrelevant content.

l: ego-graphs, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: An ego-graph is a K-hop neighborhood centered around a node. GRAG assigns each K-hop ego-graph a unique identifier, encodes it for indexing, and retrieves the most relevant ego-graphs for a query.

l: divide-and-conquer strategy, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: The divide-and-conquer strategy treats a retrieved subgraph as a union of partial neighborhoods around important nodes. It approximates the overall objective by summing the relevance of individual neighborhood subgraphs and selecting top-ranked key nodes.

l: retrieval-then-pruning approach, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: The retrieval-then-pruning approach limits the retrieval space to |V| ego-graphs rather than the full direct-search space of 2|V|+|E|. It retrieves promising neighborhoods first and then reduces redundant nodes and edges through pruning.

l: graph view, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: The graph view of textual graphs learns representations of textual graphs as soft prompts. It is used to preserve how texts are connected.

l: text view, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: The text view of textual graphs converts a textual graph into hierarchical text descriptions as hard prompts. It is used to retain how connections are narrated.

l: textual subgraphs, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: A textual subgraph is selected from the set of subgraphs of graph G to maximize generation quality. It can be formed as a union of induced subgraphs on selected key nodes and their selected K-hop neighbors.

l: key node, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: A key node is an important node that forms part of the backbone of a retrieved textual subgraph. GRAG selects top-ranked key nodes to determine which neighborhoods are combined.

l: neighborhood, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: A neighborhood consists of a node and selected nodes within K hops. GRAG encodes neighborhoods surrounding each node offline, retrieves promising candidates, and prunes them into query-relevant subgraphs.

l: textual graph, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: Graph G is the textual graph from which GRAG retrieves subgraphs. Its K-hop ego-graphs are indexed and ranked as candidate textual subgraphs.

l: learnable pruner, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: The learnable pruner refines selected neighborhoods by carving them into subgraphs that are relevant to the query and beneficial to the task.

l: PLM, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: The pre-trained language model converts the text attributes of nodes and edges into embeddings. It also encodes the query into a vector used for semantic relevance calculations.

l: graph embedding, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: A graph embedding is produced for each indexed subgraph by applying mean pooling to the pre-trained language model embeddings of its node and edge text attributes. The embedding has dimension d and is stored for retrieval.

l: query, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: The query is encoded by the same pre-trained language model as the subgraphs. Its embedding is compared with each K-hop ego-graph embedding using cosine similarity to identify the top-N relevant subgraphs.

l: generation quality, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4 .. 4.1
s: Generation quality is the objective used to evaluate a retrieved textual subgraph. The optimal subgraph is defined as the one that maximizes the function measuring this quality.

l: GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, opening
s: The unit concerns retrieving and refining subgraphs from graph G according to their semantic relevance to a query. The subset SN(G) contains the N subgraphs with the highest relevance. Textual Subgraph Soft Pruning uses two Multilayer Perceptrons to assign scaling factors to nodes and edges based on their element-wise distance from the query. The masked subgraphs are merged into an optimal subgraph structure tailored to the query with linear complexity.

l: query, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, opening
s: The query is encoded along with text attributes and is used to measure the semantic relevance of subgraphs. Its encoded representation is also compared with node and edge representations to determine their soft-pruning scaling factors.

l: textual graph, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, opening
s: Graph G provides the subgraphs from which semantically relevant candidates are retrieved and refined for a query.

l: subgraphs, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, opening
s: Subgraphs are ranked by cosine similarity to the query, and the N highest-scoring subgraphs form SN(G). Their nodes and edges are subsequently assigned adaptive scaling factors to reduce the influence of irrelevant entities.

l: Textual Subgraph Soft Pruning, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, opening
s: Textual Subgraph Soft Pruning minimizes the influence of irrelevant nodes and edges that remain in retrieved subgraphs. It uses distance from the query to softly mask entities, with farther nodes or edges receiving scalars closer to 0.

l: Multilayer Perceptrons, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, opening
s: Two Multilayer Perceptrons learn scaling factors for nodes and edges. One processes the distance between node and query representations, while the other processes the distance between edge and query representations.

l: optimal textual subgraph ˆg, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, opening
s: The optimal subgraph structure is produced by merging the adaptively masked subgraphs in SN(G). It is tailored to the query and is obtained with linear complexity.

l: GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: Textual Graph Augmented Generation provides large language models with two complementary views of a textual graph: a text view and a graph view. The text view converts retrieved ego-graphs into hierarchical descriptions by separating tree edges from additional edges, while the graph view uses a Graph Neural Network with relevance scaling factors to encode a soft pruned subgraph. An MLPϕ3 aligns graph embeddings with the large language model’s text-vector space, and the query plus hierarchical description are converted into text embeddings. Generation uses the concatenated graph and text embeddings conditioned on the retrieved subgraph and the query.

l: Textual Graph Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: It provides large language models with complementary text and graph views of a textual graph. It combines hierarchical text descriptions with graph embeddings during generation.

l: textual graph, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: It is represented through both textual information and topological information. Retrieved textual subgraphs are converted into hierarchical descriptions and graph embeddings.

l: text view, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: It converts retrieved textual ego-graphs into hierarchical descriptions that preserve textual and topological information. It provides the large language model with a query and the resulting description as a hard prompt.

l: graph view, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: It encodes the topological information of a textual graph with a Graph Neural Network. It uses relevance scaling factors to control message passing over a soft pruned subgraph.

l: large language model, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: It can reason over graphs, particularly when texts are organized in hierarchical structures such as trees. It receives concatenated graph and text embeddings to guide generation.

l: ego-graphs, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: It is split into a tree part rooted at the ego node and an edge set containing edges not included in the tree. Breadth-First Search is used on it to find the tree part.

l: tree, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: It is distinguished from an ego-graph by lacking additional edges connecting nodes within the same level or across multiple levels. A tree rooted at the ego node is obtained as part of the ego-graph conversion.

l: Breadth-First Search, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: It is applied to each retrieved ego-graph to find the tree part rooted at the ego node.

l: hierarchical description, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: It is produced by performing a pre-order traversal of the tree and appending visited node and edge texts with a relation template. Texts of the remaining edges are inserted into the description, which retains textual and topological information.

l: hard prompts, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: It is the concatenation of the query and the hierarchical description of the textual subgraph. It is provided to the large language model.

l: Graph Neural Network, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: It encodes graph topological information and performs message passing over node and edge features. Its message passing is controlled by learned relevance scaling factors.

l: optimal textual subgraph ˆg, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: It is represented through learned relevance scaling factors to reduce the influence of irrelevant entities during encoding. Its representation is used as the soft prompt.

l: soft prompts, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: It is formed from the representation of the soft pruned subgraph. It provides graph information to the large language model during generation.

l: relevance scaling factors, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: They scale node features and edge attributes during message passing in the Graph Neural Network. They are learned according to the relevance between nodes and edges and the query.

l: MLPϕ3, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: It aligns the graph embeddings with the large language model’s text-vector space. It maps the Graph Neural Network output into vectors of dimension dLLM.

l: graph embeddings, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: They are produced from the retrieved subgraph by the Graph Neural Network and then aligned by MLPϕ3. They aggregate topological information for generation.

l: text embeddings, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: They are obtained by using the text embedder of the large language model to convert the hard prompt. They are concatenated with the aligned graph embeddings before transformer processing.

l: query, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: It is used with the hierarchical description to form the hard prompt. It also guides the relevance scaling factors and conditions generation.

l: generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 4.2
s: It is guided by the retrieved subgraph and the original query. It conditions each output token on the concatenation of aligned graph embeddings and text embeddings.

l: GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 5 / 5.1 .. 5.4
s: The Experiments evaluate GRAG on the GraphQA benchmark, using WebQSP for knowledge graph question answering and ExplaGraphs for common-sense reasoning. GRAG outperforms standard RAG retrievers and LLM baselines, achieving WebQSP Hit@1 of 0.7236 and ExplaGraphs accuracy of 0.9223 without LLM fine-tuning. Results show that graph-aware retrieval, graph encoding, soft pruning, and textual graph descriptions are important for graph multi-hop reasoning. The study also finds that 2-hop ego-graphs generally outperform 1-hop ego-graphs, while retrieving too many subgraphs or using larger subgraphs can introduce irrelevant information and reduce performance.

l: Experiments, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 5 / 5.1 .. 5.4
s: The Experiments evaluate graph reasoning methods on WebQSP and ExplaGraphs, comparing GRAG, RAG with multiple retrievers, G-Retriever, and LLM baselines. They also study transferability, ego-graph size, hallucinations, and the contributions of retrieval, graph encoding, soft pruning, and graph descriptions.

l: GraphQA benchmark, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 5 / 5.1 .. 5.4
s: The GraphQA benchmark is used to evaluate models that must comprehend textual graph context to answer questions. It includes WebQSP and ExplaGraphs.

l: WebQSP, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 5 / 5.1 .. 5.4
s: WebQSP is described as a large-scale, multi-hop knowledge graph question answering dataset with averages of 4,700 graphs, 1,370.89 nodes, 4,252.37 edges, and 100,627 tokens. GRAG achieves 0.5022 F1, 0.7236 Hit@1, and 0.5099 Recall on it without LLM fine-tuning.

l: ExplaGraphs, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 5 / 5.1 .. 5.4
s: ExplaGraphs is a common-sense reasoning dataset focused on predicting positions in debates, averaging 2,766 graphs, 5.17 nodes, 4.25 edges, and 1,396 tokens. GRAG achieves 0.9223 accuracy without fine-tuning, and a GRAG model trained on WebQSP reaches 0.4540 accuracy when transferred to ExplaGraphs.

l: GRAG, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 5 / 5.1 .. 5.4
s: GRAG retrieves textual subgraphs and incorporates topological information into LLM generation. It outperforms the tested RAG retrievers and LLM baselines, and its performance benefits from graph encoding, soft pruning, textual graph descriptions, and carefully controlled 2-hop ego-graph retrieval.

l: Naive Retrieval-Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 5 / 5.1 .. 5.4
s: RAG with BM25, MiniLM-L12-v2, LaBSE, mContriever, and E5 improves LLM performance over the LLM-only baseline, but it underperforms graph-aware approaches because these retrievers do not retrieve topological information.

l: G-Retriever, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 5 / 5.1 .. 5.4
s: G-Retriever aggregates topological information as soft prompts and outperforms the tested text-only retrievers. However, it does not consider topology during retrieval and performs below GRAG on both datasets.

l: Llama2-7b, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 5 / 5.1 .. 5.4
s: Llama2-7b is the LLM used in the main comparisons, including the frozen and LoRA fine-tuned baselines. Its LLM-only results are 0.4148 Hit@1 on WebQSP and 0.3394 accuracy on ExplaGraphs.

l: fine-tuned LLM, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 5 / 5.1 .. 5.4
s: The LLM performs poorly when all graph information is placed in the prompt without retrieval, showing that redundant graph information can harm generation. GRAG substantially improves its performance without requiring fine-tuning, while fine-tuning provides only marginal additional gains when GRAG is already used.

l: graph multi-hop reasoning, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 5 / 5.1 .. 5.4
s: Graph multi-hop reasoning benefits from retrieving subgraphs that preserve graph topology rather than retrieving individual entities based only on text. GRAG is evaluated as a strategy for improving this capability.

l: knowledge graph question answering, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 5 / 5.1 .. 5.4
s: Knowledge graph question answering is evaluated primarily with WebQSP using F1 Score, Hit@1, and Recall. GRAG achieves the strongest reported performance among the compared methods without LLM fine-tuning.

l: common-sense reasoning, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 5 / 5.1 .. 5.4
s: Common-sense reasoning is evaluated with ExplaGraphs using accuracy. GRAG reaches 0.9223 accuracy, compared with 0.3394 for the LLM-only baseline and 0.8927 for the LoRA fine-tuned LLM.

s: Retrieval improves generation by reducing the negative effects of redundant graph information. The results favor retrieving textual subgraphs with topology over text-only retrieval, although adding too many subgraphs can introduce irrelevant information and reduce performance.

s: Soft pruning removes irrelevant entities when retrieved textual subgraphs are encoded into graph tokens. Removing soft pruning lowers WebQSP Hit@1 from 0.7275 to 0.5671, indicating that pruning is especially important for dense graphs.

s: The graph encoder embeds retrieved graph context for the LLM. Removing it reduces WebQSP Hit@1 from 0.7275 to 0.5835, showing that textual descriptions of node and edge relationships alone are insufficient.

s: GRAG searches over K-hop ego-graphs, with 2-hop ego-graphs consistently outperforming 1-hop ego-graphs when the same number are retrieved. Larger subgraphs can take more time, become vulnerable to oversmoothing, and introduce irrelevant information when too many are used.

s: Hit@1 is one of the primary WebQSP evaluation metrics. GRAG obtains 0.7236 Hit@1 without fine-tuning and 0.7275 with LoRA fine-tuning, compared with 0.4148 for the LLM-only baseline.

l: GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 6
s: The paper introduces Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation (GRAG) to extend Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to graph-based scenarios. GRAG enhances Large Language Models (LLMs) by retrieving query-relevant textual subgraphs through a divide-and-conquer strategy using K-hop ego-graphs and soft pruning. It provides graph and text views of a textual graph, improving contextual understanding and performance, especially for detailed, multi-hop reasoning. The approach addresses the NP-hardness of exhaustive subgraph search, and a frozen LLM enhanced by GRAG can outperform fine-tuned LLMs at lower training cost.

l: GRAG, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 6

l: textual graph, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 6
s: A textual graph is presented to LLMs through two complementary views: a graph view and a text view. These views support a more comprehensive understanding of the graph context.

l: graph multi-hop reasoning, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, 6
s: Multi-hop reasoning is a scenario in which GRAG provides particularly strong improvements over LLM and RAG-based LLM baselines. The approach is effective for tasks requiring detailed reasoning on textual graphs.

s: This unit discusses a limitation of GRAG, a framework for graph context-aware generation. Its textual subgraph retrieval depends on the quality of the initial node ranking and pruning mechanism. When graph structure or node importance is difficult to estimate, retrieval performance may be suboptimal. The work was supported by multiple National Science Foundation and NIH grants.

s: This unit describes how a 2-hop ego-graph is converted into a hierarchical textual representation and compares RAG-based retrievers on WebQSP and ExplaGraphs. It details implementation settings involving SentenceBert, GAT, Llama-2-7b-hf, and LoRA, and explains that GRAG uses graph topology and retrieved K-hop ego-graphs. The experiments find that increasing the number of retrieved entities generally helps until performance plateaus or declines because irrelevant information can impair generation.

l: 2-hop ego-graph, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, A / A.1 .. A.4
s: A 2-hop ego-graph is transformed into a nested, indented list whose hierarchy mirrors the graph structure and preserves node connections, textual information, and citation references.

s: The hierarchical description represents graph levels through indentation and nested nodes. It retains descriptive text or titles associated with nodes while making parent-child relationships and connectivity explicit.

s: RAG-based retrievers are evaluated on WebQSP and ExplaGraphs using different top-k retrieval settings. Their performance generally improves as more entities are retrieved up to a point, after which it may plateau or decline.

s: WebQSP is evaluated with Hit@1 across top-3, top-5, top-10, top-15, and top-20 retrieval settings. Retrieval performance generally increases with more retrieved entities, although some models decline slightly at larger values of k.

s: BM25 scores documents using term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document length. Its WebQSP Hit@1 increases from 0.3722 at top-3 to 0.4287 at top-20, while its ExplaGraphs Accuracy ranges from 0.5704 to 0.6011.

s: E5 uses contrastive pretraining with a bi-encoder architecture, optimizing similarity for relevant pairs and distinguishing irrelevant pairs with in-batch negatives. Its WebQSP Hit@1 ranges from 0.4404 to 0.4705, while its ExplaGraphs Accuracy ranges from 0.5921 to 0.6011.

s: GRAG replaces hard prompts with texts of retrieved entities and represents the soft prompt with tokens generated from retrieved K-hop ego-graphs. l: number of retrieved entities, GRAG: Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation, A / A.1 .. A.4

l: Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation, Knowledge Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for LLM-based Recommendation / Abstract
s: Shijie Wang and colleagues study LLM-based recommendation and its use in recommender systems. They identify hallucinations and insufficient up-to-date, domain-specific knowledge as limitations of Large Language Models in this setting. They propose K-RagRec, a retrieval-augmented framework that retrieves high-quality, up-to-date structural information from an external knowledge graph to improve recommendation generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of their method.

s: Recommender systems help alleviate information overload across various user-oriented online services. The unit presents K-RagRec as a method for improving recommendation generation.

s: Large Language Models have achieved remarkable results and show potential for next-generation recommender systems. In LLM-based recommendation, they are limited by hallucinations and a lack of up-to-date and domain-specific knowledge.

s: Retrieval-Augmented Generation uses external knowledge sources to enhance the understanding and generation of Large Language Models. The unit states that vanilla Retrieval-Augmented Generation methods can introduce noise and overlook structural relationships in knowledge.

s: K-RagRec is a retrieval-augmented framework proposed to facilitate recommendation generation by incorporating structure information from an external knowledge graph. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness.
